apush-leq-0015.comparison: The evidence shows difference in economy and daily life alongside shared political and religious frameworks — the regions diverged in how they made a living while keeping English institutions.
apush-leq-0015.complexity: Distinctness varied by region and grew over time: the Chesapeake and New England diverged earliest and most sharply, while the middle colonies were distinct precisely because they mixed peoples; and shared identity persisted even as economies split.
apush-leq-0015.context: The colonies were founded in the 1600s for different reasons — profit in the Chesapeake, a godly community in New England, refuge and trade in the middle colonies — and grew through Atlantic trade and the wars that shaped the Atlantic world.
apush-leq-0015.evidence_difference: Tobacco plantations in the Chesapeake worked by bound labor; Puritan town meetings and tight-knit towns in New England; wheat farming and many peoples (Germans, Scots-Irish, Dutch, Swedes) in the middle colonies; rice and indigo in the lower South, sugar in the West Indies.
apush-leq-0015.evidence_shared: English common law, elected assemblies (House of Burgesses, town meetings, colonial assemblies), and Protestant faith ran through all the regions.
apush-leq-0015.thesis: By 1754 the regions of British North America had developed clearly distinct identities — different economies, societies, and religious cultures — but those differences were partial, because the regions still shared English law, elected assemblies, and a broadly Protestant culture.

apush-saq-0042.a: The Halfway Covenant of 1662 loosened church membership rules, letting the children of church members be baptized even if their parents had not joined the church. By 1692, Salem showed the other side of Puritan religion: fear of the devil led to accusations against more than 100 people and the execution of 20.
apush-saq-0042.b: Fewer second-generation Puritans had joined the church, so their children could not be baptized and the parents could not vote. The covenant kept those families inside the church by baptizing their children.
apush-saq-0042.c: Salem shows Puritan authority could turn fear into deadly punishment, executing 20 people on accusations of witchcraft. That overreach is the limit: authority that claims to judge the soul ended up killing on suspicion, and it could not tell true witchcraft from fear.

apush-saq-0043.a: The Fundamental Orders set out the government of Connecticut, ordering yearly General Assemblies or Courts to meet and govern the colony.
apush-saq-0043.b: The Orders put government in writing and made it rest on regular assemblies, so rule came from an agreed written frame rather than from a king or a governor alone.
apush-saq-0043.c: Connecticut's government was set by a written agreement of the settlers with regular assemblies, while Massachusetts Bay tied government to the church: only male church members could vote, so most men were shut out of decisions.

apush-saq-0044.a: The painting shows Bacon's Rebellion of 1676, when Nathaniel Bacon's followers burned Jamestown.
apush-saq-0044.b: Frontier farmers wanted protection from Native raids, but Governor Berkeley refused to let them fight Native peoples on the frontier. (This cause is not visible in the painting itself; it comes from the lesson.)
apush-saq-0044.c: The rebellion frightened Virginia's leaders because poor whites and free Black people had fought together under Bacon. Afterward the colony moved toward laws that divided poor whites from enslaved Black people and tied slavery to race. (This consequence is not visible in the painting itself; it comes from the lesson.)

apush-saq-0045.a: Georgia was founded as a colony for the 'deserving poor' — debtors and others who had fallen on hard times in England. It was also meant as a military buffer between South Carolina and Spanish Florida.
apush-saq-0045.b: Georgia had no assembly at first, while other colonies had elected assemblies. Its settlers were also expected to serve as soldiers, a military duty other colonies did not impose.
apush-saq-0045.c: Georgia struggled under the trustees' rules, and its military buffer role needed the Crown's support. The trustees ceded Georgia to the Crown in 1752, and it became a royal colony.
